name: Marco Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead bass players in a jazz orchestra, teach at a city arts school and record short bass parts for adverts. I have a music master's and a good ear for when a band is rushing, but I still count the bars before a difficult entrance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the home side of that schedule?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lena works in a library, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is good, we have eight months of expenses saved, and several venues and schools hire nearby. I use AI occasionally for set lists after another player has tested a tool, then check every tune against the band book.

I'd tell the band the **drummer's pulse** still needs listening.
think: Our **eight-month reserve** and paid teaching cover a slow advert invoice.
I use **AI occasionally** for set lists and compare each tune with the signed programme.
do: Renew **three paid teaching days** and confirm signed winter shows this week.
Save **one hundred** from a cleared advert fee after transport and school costs.
feel: I feel **calm** because a delayed invoice cannot disrupt essential bills.
S0.quote: A missing tune can leave a singer waiting in silence.
fieldNote: His **higher pay** and eight months saved make one late recording invoice manageable.
His **occasional AI use** follows a colleague's trial and a manual programme check.

steps.text: Renew three paid arts-school days and confirm signed winter shows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that faster set lists are convenient, but a player still has to hear the drummer. The job is making a room move together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI mostly stalls, the school and live dates should keep paying. Eight months saved and Lena's library wage cover a slow advert invoice, though I still read the mortgage date each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll renew my three paid teaching days and confirm the orchestra's signed winter programme. When the next advert fee clears, I'll move one hundred into our reserve after instrument transport and the children's school costs are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this version. One delayed invoice cannot make us abandon the band or the children's plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the late studio invoice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A studio took five extra weeks to settle a bass part in June. We paid the mortgage from the usual account and did not use the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the set-list tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use a tool to order the set list after a colleague tries it. I compare the result with the signed programme. A missing tune can leave a singer waiting in silence.

I'd bring **fee sheets** to the musicians association.

Listen **against the original**; require written player consent and stop for false notes or files leaving the studio.
feel: I feel **anxious** because clients may stop paying for hours I still work.
S1.quote: I will learn a proven tool, but I need a fee that pays the player.
fieldNote: His **advert and planning fees** account for a third of income at risk.
His **new tool trial** needs paid instruction, owned material, licence, local storage, manual comparison and written consent.

steps.text: Bring ten recording invoices and new offers to musicians association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the studio and school what happens to paid arrangement and rehearsal-planning hours. I would bring the last fee sheet to the musicians association before signing a new contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third of my pay comes from advert bass parts and planning sets, and clients may buy fewer hours. Eight months saved gives us time to adjust, but it cannot make a lasting loss of that income painless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten recording invoices with the new fee offers and take them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll try a new AI bass-isolation tool, which separates bass from other recorded instruments, only after a paid studio demonstration, on my own nameless take with a licence for paid use and approved local storage; I'll listen against the original and stop if it invents notes or sends the file outside the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the client paying for fewer hours even if the tool sounds clever. I will learn a proven tool, but I need a fee that pays the player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose recording could go into the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not put another player's take or a pupil's lesson into a trial without written permission. A false low note can spoil the whole arrangement, so I will return to the original if the split is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the association request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association can ask for a written minimum live-player fee and a limit on free revisions. I'll bring invoices rather than guess the studio's margin.

fieldNote: His **2028 arrangement loss** precedes robot bass playing around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the jazz players that AGI by 2028 can arrange a chart before robots can play bass around 2031. I would ask for next season's live fees in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid screen work may shrink at once, while audiences still pay for a live band. If advert fees halve, our eight-month reserve buys a search period, but the mortgage will not wait forever for another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll separate school, venue and advert pay and request signed next-season band dates. In the first year after 2028, if advert fees halve and a school day is cut, I'll apply for a posted ensemble-director role at another local school only if my master's qualifies, pickup works and written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I'll keep the current school and band until another offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a combined cut, but several local employers and savings give me ways to act. A familiar venue is not a paid vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is another school role actually open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One school posted a director job last year and filled it. I'll ask when another opens, but I will not put a closed post in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if both fees fall together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If both teaching and advert fees fall, Lena and I would ask the lender about temporary terms before arrears. We would compare the total added interest before agreeing.

Seek **posted sound work** after 2031 only if adverts fall, certificate qualifies, written net pay improves budget and pickup fits.

S3.quote: I need a real paid shift after training, not just a certificate.
fieldNote: His **five-year training** requires grant, venue acceptance, college equipment and child-pickup coverage.
His **sound job** requires a posted shift, accepted certificate and written net pay after travel before he leaves current work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players five years gives time to learn the sound desk if someone pays for training. I would ask which local venues recognise the college's live-sound certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could arrange bass parts and plan sets, while robots able to handle stage gear follow around 2034. Ordinary software may cut paid editing earlier. I need a real paid shift after training, not just a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the technical college if a grant covers its live-sound course, venues accept the certificate and class evenings fit Lena's library rota for pickup. I'll enrol only if all three are confirmed and I can use college equipment instead of buying a desk. In the first year after 2031, if advert fees fall, I'll seek a posted paid sound shift only if the certificate qualifies me, written net pay after travel improves our household budget and pickup still works; I'll keep band and school work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about fees fading while I study. Eight months saved gives room for an accepted course, but I will not pay for an unrecognised one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy equipment or extra childcare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college has a rehearsal desk and microphones. If classes fall on Lena's late library night, I'll wait for another intake rather than spend the reserve on extra childcare.

transcript.text: Has a venue posted a paid sound role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A venue manager said they sometimes need a sound hand, but no job is posted. I will ask for a written rate and actual opening before changing the band calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band a decade can support a properly paid jazz series, if the venue and players see the numbers first. I would ask for sponsor and insurance terms in writing before announcing a night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, I will still need a wage, and robot bassists could reach stages around 2039. Advert fees may thin well before then, so the series cannot eat our mortgage reserve just to look busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the arts hall about a monthly jazz evening only if a sponsor's money clears room and insurance, the hall signs its terms and fourteen prepaid tickets cover agreed player rates. By 2036 I'll aim to move our reserve from eight to twelve months by saving one hundred from each extra paid school workshop after childcare, players and the mortgage are paid. In the first year after AGI, I'll continue the evening only if the sponsor renews, written hall terms hold and fourteen tickets still pay the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about advert fees falling before a decade passes, though savings give us a careful way to test live nights. I will not ask my children to fill seats so the numbers appear to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must happen before publicity, and if nine tickets sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before the first poster, sponsor funds must clear and the hall must sign insurance terms. Every player sees and accepts the rate first; if only nine tickets sell, I'll refund buyers and keep the school work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a pupil recording advertise the evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not use a pupil's rehearsal recording in an advert without written family permission. A live open rehearsal can show the music without posting a child online.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because adverts and school hours could fall together before another paid director post opens. Signed band dates, a qualifying vacancy and the lender's full costs would help us protect the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how many tickets pay the musicians before a concert becomes a promise. A poster is not a payroll for the band.

headlineQuote: A poster is not a payroll for the band.
portrait: Marco is a **43-year-old bass leader** with a music master's, partner, two children and a mortgage.
His **higher pay** and eight-month reserve buffer delays, while advert and planning work remain exposed.
He uses **AI occasionally** and tests new bass isolation only after paid instruction, local storage and listening checks.
He pursues **funded sound training** and a covered jazz series while retaining paid school work until another offer.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could cut advert and school pay together before another director role opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed band dates**, a posted qualifying role and full lender costs would help guard the mortgage.
